apa.quarto.pdf() on the next, inside a code chunk whose settings lines you

  #| label: an identifier starting with "tbl-" so you can cross-reference the
            table in text (e.g. @tbl-correlation)
Every table chunk also carries #| message: false and #| warning: true.
The first keeps package-loading chatter out of the document; the second

That #| label line is the only one most chunks below need, and it is not
optional. Without one starting "tbl-", Quarto builds no table float for the
chunk at all, so there is no number, no title and no note, however you try
to supply them.

rendered PDF was written by apaTables from the table itself. Let it do that.
It knows what the table contains, so it describes it correctly and keeps
the italics right, and it writes the title again every time you render. A
title you type by hand stops being true the moment you change the analysis

ONE page, the d-values table, writes its own title and note instead, because

Edit the title and author above, and the captions and notes below, to suit your

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(apaTables)
# afex is loaded here, out of sight, so the one-time startup notices from
# its dependencies stay out of the rendered document
if (requireNamespace("afex", quietly = TRUE)) library(afex)
```

# Correlation table

`apa.cor.table()` produces a correlation table with means and standard
deviations. Build it on one line, then display it with `apa.quarto.pdf()` on
the next.

**This is the ordinary way, and it is the whole of it.** The chunk below writes
one settings line, `#| label`, and nothing about the title or the note.
Everything you see above and below the table in the rendered PDF -- the number,
the italic title, and the note explaining *N*, *M*, *SD* and the confidence
intervals -- was written by apaTables from the table itself.

The `#| label` line is not optional, and it must start with `tbl-`: without
one, Quarto builds no table float for the chunk at all, so there is no number,
no title and no note, however you try to supply them. It is also what lets you
write `@tbl-correlation` in a sentence and have Quarto fill in the number.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-correlation
#| message: false
#| warning: true
my_table <- apa.cor.table(attitude)
apa.quarto.pdf(my_table)
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

# A wide correlation table, on a rotated page

The correlation table earlier in this document has seven variables and is
narrow enough for an ordinary upright page. (Being too TALL is not a problem
that needs solving: a table that does not fit in the space left on a page
moves to the next page whole, and a table taller than a page continues onto
the next one with its column headings repeated.) This one has nine variables
and is too WIDE, which is a
different matter entirely: no amount of continuing onto another page makes a
table narrower. So the table is on the next page, and that page is rotated.
The table is about 7.0 inches wide,
and an upright page gives a table only 6.5 inches. When this document was
rendered, apaTables measured the table, found it would not fit, and asked
apaquarto for a rotated (landscape) page. The table is printed at full size
there: no column is dropped and nothing is shrunk. A rotated page cannot also
carry this upright paragraph, which is why the table moved to a page of its
own.

**There is nothing in this document's `.qmd` source file that asks for the
rotation.** The code chunk that produces the table is an ordinary code chunk,
and the settings block at the top of the source file says nothing about page
orientation. You do not have to predict
which of your tables will need a rotated page -- apaTables measures each one
as the document renders and asks for a rotated page only when it is needed.
That is why the earlier correlation table stayed upright while this one
turned: the decision is made per table, from its actual width.

The same thing happens to the hierarchical regression table later in this
document, for the same reason: any apaTables table that measures too wide
for the upright page gets a rotated one.

If you ever need to overrule the measurement, every builder takes a
`landscape` argument: `landscape = TRUE` forces a rotated page,
`landscape = FALSE` forbids one, and the default measures.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-correlation-wide
#| message: false
#| warning: true
my_table <- apa.cor.table(dating_wide)
apa.quarto.pdf(my_table)
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Regression table

`apa.reg.table()` summarizes one or more `lm()` regression models. Build the
table, then send it to `apa.quarto.pdf()` -- its title and note are
generated automatically, so the chunk needs nothing beyond the label.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-regression
#| message: false
#| warning: true
blk1 <- lm(sales ~ adverts + airplay, data = album)
my_table <- apa.reg.table(blk1)
apa.quarto.pdf(my_table)
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Hierarchical (blocks) regression, on a rotated page

`apa.reg.table()` accepts two or more models to compare regression blocks.
Comparing blocks adds columns, so a blocks table is wider than a
single-model one -- **and adding more predictors does not widen a regression
table at all, because predictors are rows.** If you want to see a regression
table on a rotated page, the blocks form is the one that gets there.

The table for this section is on the next page, and that page is rotated. The table is about 7.1 inches wide; an upright (portrait) page gives a table 6.5 inches. So when this document was rendered, apaTables measured the table, found it would not stand upright, and asked apaquarto for a rotated page. The table is at its full size on that page; no column is cut off and nothing is shrunk. There is nothing in this document's `.qmd` source file that asks for the rotation. The code chunk below is an ordinary code chunk, and the settings block at the top of the source file says nothing about page orientation. A rotated page cannot also carry this upright paragraph, which is why the table moved to a page of its own.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-regblocks
#| message: false
#| warning: true
blkA <- lm(sales ~ adverts + airplay, data = album)
blkB <- lm(sales ~ adverts + airplay + I(adverts * airplay), data = album)
my_table <- apa.reg.table(blkA, blkB)
apa.quarto.pdf(my_table)
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Standardized mean differences (d values)

`apa.d.table()` reports all pairwise standardized mean differences for a single
independent variable.

**This is the one page in this document that does not let apaTables write the
title and note.** Every table before it wrote a `#| label` line and nothing
else. Here `title =` and `note =` are passed to `apa.quarto.pdf()` instead, and
what they say replaces what the table would have said -- compare the title on
this page with the ones on the pages before it. Markdown notation such as `*M*`
still renders as italics, so a hand-written note can carry the same formatting.

**Use this only when you genuinely need your own wording.** The generated title
and note describe the table that is actually there and are re-derived every time
you render; anything you type here stays as you typed it, so it can quietly stop
matching the analysis above it. That is the whole reason the rest of this
document leaves them alone.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dvalues
#| message: false
#| warning: true
my_table <- apa.d.table(iv = dose, dv = libido, data = viagra)
apa.quarto.pdf(my_table,
    title = "Means, Standard Deviations, and My Own d-Value Title",
    note  = "*M* = mean. *SD* = standard deviation. My own note describing the *d*-values and confidence intervals.")
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

# ANOVA table

`apa.aov.table()` produces an ANOVA F-table from an `lm()` model. The
`contrasts` option is set before fitting the model so the sums of squares
match common software.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-anova
#| message: false
#| warning: true
options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly"))
lm_output <- lm(libido ~ dose, data = viagra)
my_table <- apa.aov.table(lm_output)
apa.quarto.pdf(my_table)
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

# One-way means and standard deviations

`apa.1way.table()` reports cell means and standard deviations for a one-way
design.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-oneway
#| message: false
#| warning: true
my_table <- apa.1way.table(iv = dose, dv = libido, data = viagra)
apa.quarto.pdf(my_table)
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Two-way means and standard deviations

`apa.2way.table()` reports cell means and standard deviations for a two-way
design.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-twoway
#| message: false
#| warning: true
my_table <- apa.2way.table(iv1 = gender, iv2 = alcohol,
                           dv = attractiveness, data = goggles)
apa.quarto.pdf(my_table)
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Repeated-measures ANOVA (afex)

`apa.afex.table()` builds an ANOVA F-table from `afex::aov_ez()` output.
This table requires two additional packages that do not come with
apaTables. If rendering stops on this page with a message that afex or
tidyr is missing, run `install.packages(c("afex", "tidyr"))` once in the
R console, then render again.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-afex
#| message: false
#| warning: true
drink_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(drink_attitude_wide,
                                  cols = beer_positive:water_neutral,
                                  names_to = c("drink", "imagery"),
                                  names_sep = "_",
                                  values_to = "attitude")
drink_long$drink <- as.factor(drink_long$drink)
drink_long$imagery <- as.factor(drink_long$imagery)
drink_results <- afex::aov_ez(id = "participant", dv = "attitude",
                              data = drink_long,
                              within = c("drink", "imagery"))
my_table <- apa.afex.table(drink_results)
apa.quarto.pdf(my_table)
```
